prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Courier Delivery Commitments by Destination (language en).
Grid: 3 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Destination" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Delivery" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Destination" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 145px
  col 2: header "Delivery › Window" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 64px
  col 3: header "Delivery › Conditions" · longest unbreakable word 94px · one-line width 1546px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Show delivery windows and the conditions that affect commitments for each destination.","reading":"Readers locate a destination, compare its delivery window with other destinations, then read across the same row for qualifications. Long conditions will determine most row heights, leaving room for destination names to wrap.","groups":["Window and Conditions belong under Delivery: the window gives the commitment, while the conditions qualify it.","Destination is the row identifier and should remain easy to scan independently of the delivery details."],"keep_intact":["Delivery windows such as 2–3 days","Unbreakable words and identifiers within destination names and conditions"],"may_wrap":["Conditions at natural word boundaries","Multiword destination names, especially Remote island areas, where row height already accommodates the conditions"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[166,85,468],"idea":"Keep destination names and delivery windows on one line while giving the remaining width to conditions."},{"name":"B","widths":[110,85,524],"idea":"Allow multiword destinations to wrap into the height created by conditions, maximizing space for the long explanatory text."},{"name":"C","widths":[200,120,399],"idea":"Give the destination and window columns generous, distinct scanning space, accepting more wrapping in conditions."}]}
